name: Childhood amnesia
statement: Adults recall almost nothing from the first three years of life, and fewer events from ages three to seven than ordinary forgetting predicts.
meaning: The claim has two halves and they are usually run together. The first is a near-absence of autobiographical memory from before about age three. The second is a shortfall from three to seven, where the count of memories falls below what a forgetting curve extended backwards would give. Two methods measure this and they answer different questions. Ask adults for their earliest memory and date it, and you get a single boundary age, traditionally placed near three and a half years. Record children talking about events at age three and re-interview them years later, and you get a forgetting rate, which puts the heaviest loss between ages seven and nine. Both findings are old, large and stable. Where the boundary sits moves with how the question is asked and with who dates the memory. What the phenomenon is caused by is not settled, and that is where the field divides.

origin.note: Freud supplied the name and the wrong span. Under the heading Infantile Amnesia he described 'the peculiar amnesia which veils from most people (not from all!) the first years of their childhood, usually the first six or eight years', and put it down to repression, in Brill's English translation. Surveys of earliest recollections predate him: Caroline Miles published A Study of Individual Psychology in the American Journal of Psychology, and Victor and C. Henri published Enquête sur les premiers souvenirs de l'enfance in L'Année Psychologique in 1896. The Henri paper says its questionnaire went out in 1895 in five journals, including the American Journal of Psychology, which is why the dates attached to this founding work vary. Miles is cited across the childhood-amnesia literature as 1893, the year its volume opened; Crossref dates the issue to January 1895.

evidence: Rubin assembled the distribution from published studies, pooling over 11,000 autobiographical memories from age 10 and younger, 10,118 of them dated to age 7 and younger. Of the memories reported from before age 11, 1.1% came from before age 3. The shape came out nearly identical for males and females and for participants of different ages. It also held across four ways of collecting the memories: cue words for memories from anywhere in the lifespan, cue words restricted to childhood, exhaustive listing of all early memories, and interviews. Rubin flags one possible exception, the interview method, which runs higher for years 3, 4 and 5 on the least data of the four. Every study he pooled was run in the United States, and he writes that data from other cultures would almost certainly differ. On the adult side the boundary sits near three. Akhtar, Justice, Morrison and Conway surveyed 6,641 people for their first memory and its age, and found a mean age at encoding of 3.2 years. Bauer and Larkina measured the same thing from the other end. Eighty-three children discussed unique recent events with their parents at a mean age of 3.29 years, 81 of them with their mothers alone and two with both parents. Subgroups were re-interviewed by an experimenter at ages 5, 6, 7, 8 and 9, giving retention intervals of two to six years. Two children produced no events meeting the recall criterion and were dropped, so the recall analyses rest on 81. Children aged 5, 6 and 7 remembered 60% or more of those events. Children aged 8 and 9 remembered fewer than 40%, F(4, 75) = 5.66, p < .01, eta-squared = .22, in an analysis of covariance controlling age at the first session. The count of children who recalled nothing at all moves the same way. At most 6% of the 5-, 6- and 7-year-olds recalled none of the age-3 events, against 37% of 8-year-olds, seven of 19, and 25% of 9-year-olds, four of 16, Fisher's exact test p = .003. Bauer and Larkina also charted cue-word memory distributions in children aged 7 to 11 and in young and middle-aged adults. The adult distributions were best fit by a power function and the children's by an exponential, which they read as a constant rate of forgetting through childhood rather than a single early cut-off. How the question is asked moves the answer. Jack and Hayne gave young adults either a request for their six earliest memories or cue words sampling different epochs. Asking for early memories yielded a higher density of events from inside the amnesic period. Their reading is that early memories stay available and become less accessible.

replication.headline: The phenomenon holds across methods, samples, cultures and both directions of study; the arguments are about the mechanism and about where exactly the boundary sits.
replication.detail: Rubin's pooled distribution is the strongest single check, because invariance across sexes, ages and four elicitation methods is what a fragile finding does not do. Prospective work in children reproduces the loss on a schedule. Peterson, Warren and Short re-interviewed children aged 4 to 13 after two years. Their dated earliest memories had shifted several months later. Younger children rarely produced the same memories and often failed to recall them even when cued. Older children stayed consistent. Peterson, Hallett and Compton-Gillingham followed 37 children across eight years with interviews at the start and after two and eight years. There was little overlap in spontaneous earliest memories across interviews. The youngest group forgot over half their initial memories. Of the content given by the former 6- to 9-year-olds, 25% to 32% was the same after eight years. For the youngest children it was under 10%, and 22% contradicted what they had said before. Reese and Robertson followed 58 children from age one and a half to age 16 across eight timepoints, with early memory interviews at 12 and 16, taken by 46 and 51 of them. The mean age of first memory rose from 40 to 52 months between those two interviews, so the loss continues through adolescence. Bauer, Larkina, Güler and Burch tracked 101 children over four annual waves, starting at ages 4, 6 and 8, with a further 34 enrolled who did not complete. Memories became more likely to survive the delay as children got older, and the rate of that increase was the same in all three cohorts, which the authors read as continuity rather than a boundary. Tustin and Hayne compared children, adolescents and adults on one timeline procedure. The proportion of memories from before age three was larger for the children and adolescents. Their single earliest memory was younger than the adults', and younger than the traditional three-and-a-half-year boundary. The boundary also moves with culture. Wang had 256 American and Chinese students report an earliest memory, and the American mean fell almost six months earlier than the Chinese. Peterson, Wang and Hou found the same gap in 225 European Canadian and 133 Chinese children aged 8, 11 and 14, and found it widening with age, with the Chinese 14-year-olds already adult-like. MacDonald, Uesiliana and Hayne compared New Zealand European, New Zealand Maori and Asian adults: Asian adults reported later memories than European adults, an effect carried entirely by Asian women, and Maori adults reported earlier memories than either group. Mullen's four questionnaire studies, 768 respondents in total, found age of earliest memory rising with birth order, slightly earlier for women than men, and earlier for Caucasian than Asian respondents.

study.cite: Rubin, D. C. (2000). The distribution of early childhood memories. Memory, 8(4), 265-269.

limits: The verdict covers the existence and the shape of the memory shortfall. It does not cover why it happens, and nothing here should be read as endorsing any mechanism. The dating is a live problem. Wang, Peterson, Khuu, Reid, Maxwell and Vincent collected five earliest memories from 32 Cornell students and 49 Memorial University students and dated the same events independently with their parents. Memories encoded before 48 months were postdated by close to 12 months in the first sample and over 6 months in the second. Later memories were predated by over 6 months in the first sample, while in the second the students and their parents agreed, F(1, 112) = 0.02, p = .89. Parents put the earlier memories at 36.5 and 34.1 months. Taking the parents' figures, or correcting the students' figures for their own telescoping, puts the first memory near 2.5 years rather than the 3.5 the authors say is commonly assumed. Their samples are small and drawn from students, and parental dating is a proxy for the truth rather than the truth. Peterson reviews two decades of her laboratory's published and unpublished data. How early an earliest memory is depends on the number of interviews, the number of memories asked for, the type of interview and what the participant did beforehand. Peterson, Murphy, Hallett and Roberts told 200 young adults that first memories usually date from age 2 or from age 4. The two groups dated their first memory to different ages, and the ages their parents gave did not differ, so the prime moved the date and not the memory. Parents supplied dates for 117 of the 200 and the rest were imputed. The neurogenesis account is animal evidence with a human gap in the middle. Akers and colleagues raised hippocampal neurogenesis after learning in adult mice and induced forgetting. Lowering it in infant mice reduced forgetting. Guinea pigs and degus, which generate most granule cells before birth, did not show infantile forgetting until neurogenesis was raised artificially. Josselyn and Frankland set this out as a hypothesis rather than a demonstration. Whether the human hippocampus generates new neurons after infancy is itself disputed. Sorrells and colleagues found young neurons declining sharply over the first year of life. They detected none in the dentate gyrus of 17 post-mortem control samples or 12 surgical samples from adults with epilepsy. Yates and colleagues scanned 26 awake infants aged 4.2 to 24.9 months during a subsequent-memory task. Hippocampal activity at encoding predicted later memory-based looking in the 13 infants older than a year and not in the 13 younger, which points at post-encoding inaccessibility rather than failure to encode. That sample showed no overall looking preference for the old items, mean 0.510, 95% CI 0.473 to 0.545. Several sources here were read as abstracts only. They are Tustin and Hayne, Jack and Hayne, Mullen, the four Peterson papers other than the cross-cultural one, Reese and Robertson, the second Bauer and Larkina paper, Josselyn and Frankland, Akers, Guskjolen, Sorrells, and all three cross-cultural papers. MacDonald and colleagues' abstract reports the direction of the cultural differences without the ages, and the month figures widely quoted for that study were not traced to it and are omitted. Three short papers were not obtained: the 2019 comment by Bauer, Baker-Ward, Krøjgaard, Peterson and Wang, the reply to it, and the 2020 corrigendum to the fictional-memory paper. Their publisher refused automated requests, and Crossref, PubMed, Europe PMC, Unpaywall, OpenAlex, JSTOR, Aarhus University's repository and Internet Archive Scholar returned records without text. Clinical claims about recovered memories of early abuse belong to false memory, entry 35. The rise on the other side of this dip belongs to the reminiscence bump, entry 117.
misreadings: The boundary is treated as the age at which memory begins. It is the age of the earliest thing an adult can still retrieve, and the prospective work shows three-year-olds holding events that seven-year-olds still have and nine-year-olds have mostly lost. Rubin's pooled distribution is quoted for the age of the earliest memory. He states that he is not addressing that question, because each participant supplies only one such memory, and restricts the paper to the distribution of early memories. A first memory is also assumed to be a memory. Akhtar and colleagues found 2,487 of 6,641 first memories, close to 40%, dated to age two or younger, and 893 of those dated to age one or younger. They argue that memories dated that early are constructions rather than recollections. Bauer, Baker-Ward, Krøjgaard, Peterson and Wang answered under the title Evidence Against Depiction as Fiction, and Akhtar and colleagues replied; the exchange is about what counts as an autobiographical memory, and it is unresolved. Freud's explanation travels with his name and does not survive the data. He put the amnesia at the first six or eight years and attributed it to repression, and the modern boundary is roughly half that span with no repression required. The mouse neurogenesis experiments are quoted as the cause of human childhood amnesia. They are causal experiments in rodents, and the human evidence for postnatal hippocampal neurogenesis is contested. Loss of access is read as erasure. Guskjolen and colleagues tagged the neurons active during fear encoding in infant mice. Stimulating those dentate gyrus neurons with light recovered the apparently lost memory up to three months later. That is what a retrieval failure looks like and not what a deleted memory looks like.
